pos: n. (capital of Denmark; where the realm was reformed by the Church Ordinance of 1537)
etymology: From Danish København, the merchants' harbour; købmand, merchant, and havn, haven.
biblical_def: Copenhagen is where the Danish Reformation became the religion of a kingdom. The evangelical preachers had presented their articles to the Herredag there in 1530; six years later Christian III won the civil war, arrested the bishops, and took their lands to the crown. On 2 September 1537 the Church Ordinance was promulgated in the city, drawn with the help of Johannes Bugenhagen of Wittenberg, who had come north for the purpose; Bugenhagen crowned the king, ordained the seven new superintendents, and reformed the university, which reopened the same year as the seminary of the realm. The dictionary records Copenhagen because the ordinance of 1537 is a national covenant in the biblical pattern: a prince standing before God with his people, binding both to a written rule. Josiah did the same thing in Jerusalem, and the chronicler describes the act with care, that he “made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments” (2Ch 34:31), performing the words of the covenant written in the book. A reformation that is not written down is not yet a reformation; it is a mood.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a covenant as a mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons to do or forbear some act; an ordinance as a rule established by authority; and to promulgate as to publish, to make known by open declaration.
webster_full: COVENANT, n. [L. convenio.] A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; stipulation.
ORDINANCE, n. [from ordain.] A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; a law or statute.
PROMULGATE, v.t. [L. promulgo.] To publish; to make known by open declaration, as laws or decrees.
REALM, n. [Fr. royaume.] A royal jurisdiction or extent of government; a kingdom; a king's dominions.
scriptures: And the king stood in his place, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments, and his testimonies, and his statutes, with all his heart, and with all his soul, to perform the words of the covenant which are written in this book.
And Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people, that they should be the LORD'S people; between the king also and the people.

And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all their heart and all their soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. And all the people stood to the covenant.
And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul;
corruption_summary: The Danish capital, where the Church Ordinance of 1537 reformed a whole kingdom under a written rule.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the modern assumption that a national establishment of religion is the whole of what the Reformation wanted, so that when the establishment decays the Reformation is thought to have failed. Denmark shows both halves. The ordinance of 1537 did real good: it put preaching, schools and poor relief on an evangelical footing in every parish. It could not and did not convert the nation, and no written rule ever will.

The principle to recover is that covenanting is a public and binding act, and that it belongs to rulers and people together. Jehoiada bound all three parties at once, making “a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people” (2Ki 11:17). Josiah's renewal was read out of a book and the people took their stand on it, so that “all the people stood to the covenant” (2Ki 23:3). Asa's generation bound themselves to the seeking itself, for “they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart” (2Ch 15:12). The covenant is the beginning of obedience, not a substitute for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew berith (H1285), a covenant; Hebrew sepher (H5612), a book or writing.
roots_lines: Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant, a compact made by passing between pieces of flesh; 2 Chronicles 34:31.
Hebrew sepher (H5612) — a writing, a book, a scroll; 2 Kings 23:3.
Hebrew karath (H3772) — to cut, and so to make a covenant; 2 Kings 11:17.
Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, to enquire diligently; 2 Chronicles 15:12.
Hebrew mitsvah (H4687) — a commandment, a precept; 2 Chronicles 34:31.
usage: “made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments” (2Ch 34:31) — the Church Ordinance, 2 September 1537.
“And all the people stood to the covenant” (2Ki 23:3) — Bugenhagen crowns the king and ordains seven superintendents.
“they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart” (2Ch 15:12) — the university reopened as the seminary of the realm.

pos: n. (cathedral city of Zealand, Denmark; ancient episcopal see and burial church of the Danish kings)
etymology: From Old Norse Hróarskelda, the spring of Hroar; kelda, a well or spring.
biblical_def: Roskilde held the greatest bishopric in Denmark and the tombs of her kings. Its bishop Joachim Ronnow was among those arrested in the revolution of 1536, and the see passed to evangelical superintendents; the brick cathedral, begun in the twelfth century, became and remains the burial church of the Danish crown, where kings and queens lie in ordered rows under the same roof as the pulpit. Niels Hemmingsen, removed from his chair at Copenhagen in 1579, was pensioned to a canonry here and died in the city in 1600. The dictionary records Roskilde because a church full of royal tombs preaches a sermon no preacher need improve. Peter, standing in Jerusalem within sight of a famous grave, used it to prove that the man in it was not the Christ, saying of David that “he is both dead and buried, and his sepulchre is with us unto this day” (Act 2:29). The argument is still good. A monarchy may be reformed, endowed and honoured, and it will still require a burial church; only one tomb in the world is empty.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a sepulchre as a grave, a tomb, a place in which the dead body of a human being is interred; a cathedral as the see or seat of a bishop; and to inter as to bury, to deposit in the earth.
webster_full: SEPULCHER, n. [L. sepulchrum.] A grave; a tomb; the place in which the dead body of a human being is interred.
CATHEDRAL, n. [L. cathedra, a seat.] The see or seat of a bishop; the principal church in a diocese.
INTER, v.t. [L. in and terra, the earth.] To bury; to inhume; to deposit in the earth, as a dead body.
MONUMENT, n. [L. monumentum.] Any thing by which the memory of a person or of an event is preserved or perpetuated; a building, stone or other thing placed for a memorial.
scriptures: Act 2:29
Men and brethren, let me freely speak unto you of the patriarch David, that he is both dead and buried, and his sepulchre is with us unto this day.
So David slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David.
His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.
Ecc 8:8

There is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit; neither hath he power in the day of death: and there is no discharge in that war; neither shall wickedness deliver those that are given to it.
corruption_summary: The greatest Danish bishopric and the burial church of her kings; Niels Hemmingsen's refuge and place of death.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation a royal burial church creates is older and quieter than any modern error: the slow transfer of reverence from God to the dynasty that patronises His worship. A church whose chief ornaments are the monuments of its benefactors must preach against its own furniture.

The principle to recover is the mortality of every ruler and the comfort that this is so. Of the best king Israel had, the record is brief: “So David slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David” (1Ki 2:10). The psalmist draws the practical conclusion against putting trust in princes, for of man he says that “His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth” (Psa 146:4), and in that very day his thoughts perish. The preacher states the limit no office evades: “There is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit” (Ecc 8:8), neither hath he power in the day of death.
roots_summary: Greek mnema (G3418), a tomb; Hebrew ruach (H7307), breath or spirit.
roots_lines: Greek mnema (G3418) — a monument, a sepulchre; Acts 2:29.
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — wind, breath, spirit; Psalm 146:4.
Hebrew qabar (H6912) — to bury, to inter; 1 Kings 2:10.
Hebrew shakab (H7901) — to lie down, and so to sleep in death; 1 Kings 2:10.
Hebrew shiltown (H7983) — power, dominion, mastery; Ecclesiastes 8:8.
usage: “he is both dead and buried, and his sepulchre is with us unto this day” (Act 2:29) — the burial church of the Danish crown.
“So David slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David” (1Ki 2:10) — Bishop Ronnow arrested in the revolution of 1536.
“His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth” (Psa 146:4) — Hemmingsen pensioned here and dead in 1600.

pos: n. (cathedral city of east Jutland, Denmark; evangelical see from 1537)
etymology: From Old Danish Århús, the house at the river mouth; å, river, and hús, house.
biblical_def: Aarhus is the cathedral city of eastern Jutland, its great brick church dedicated to St Clement, and one of the seven sees given an evangelical superintendent under the ordinance of 1537. Its reformation was less dramatic than Malmo's and more typical: no civic rising, no printed manifesto, but a slow replacement of the mass by preaching, of the Latin breviary by the Danish psalm, and of the altar's sacrifice by the pulpit's proclamation. The chapter school became a Latin school and the diocese was visited and catechised for a century afterwards. The dictionary records Aarhus because the ordinary parish reformation is the one most easily forgotten and the one that actually held the North. Its whole substance can be put in a sentence Paul wrote to a city far more sophisticated than Aarhus: “For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1Co 2:2). Where that determination governs a pulpit, the furniture of worship simplifies itself without a decree, because everything that competed with the cross has lost its reason to be there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to crucify as to nail to a cross, to put to death by nailing the hands and feet to a cross; a stumblingblock as any cause of stumbling, and figuratively a cause of error or sin; and to preach as to pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject.
webster_full: CRUCIFY, v.t. [L. crucifigo.] To nail to a cross; to put to death by nailing the hands and feet to a cross or gibbet.
STUMBLINGBLOCK, n. Any cause of stumbling; that which causes to err, or any occasion of sinning.
PREACH, v.i. [L. praedico.] To pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject, or from a religious text.
DETERMINE, v.t. [L. determino.] To fix on; to settle; to decide; to resolve; to conclude.
scriptures: For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;
Gal 6:14
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world.
Act 5:42
And daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: Jutland's eastern cathedral city, one of the seven evangelical sees of 1537, reformed by preaching rather than by rising.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the instinct to present the gospel as something other than a crucified man, on the ground that the cross offends. Paul knew that it offends and said so, and he preached it anyway, because the offence is the point at which the gospel stops being a philosophy. A pulpit that has learned to avoid the offence has nothing left to preach that the hearer could not have reasoned out on his own.

The principle to recover is the centrality and the scandal of the cross together. Paul states both in one breath: “But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness” (1Co 1:23). He will boast of nothing else, saying that God forbid he “should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal 6:14). And the first church kept at it without interval or variation, for “daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ” (Act 5:42).
roots_summary: Greek stauroo (G4717), to crucify; Greek skandalon (G4625), a stumblingblock.
roots_lines: Greek stauroo (G4717) — to crucify, to impale on a cross; 1 Corinthians 1:23.
Greek skandalon (G4625) — a trap, a stumblingblock, an occasion of falling; 1 Corinthians 1:23.
Greek stauros (G4716) — a cross, the instrument of crucifixion; Galatians 6:14.
Greek krino (G2919) — to judge, to decide, to determine; 1 Corinthians 2:2.
Greek kauchaomai (G2744) — to boast, to glory; Galatians 6:14.

“But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness” (1Co 1:23) — one of the seven sees of the 1537 ordinance.
“daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ” (Act 5:42) — a century of visitation and catechising.

pos: n. (duchy and town on the Danish-German border; a bilingual territory reformed early and governed from Haderslev)
etymology: From Old Norse Slesvik, the bay of the river Sli; German Schleswig.
biblical_def: Slesvig was the Danish realm's border country, Danish in the north and German in the south, and the Reformation reached it before it reached Denmark proper because Duke Christian held part of it as his own. The duchy therefore had to do from the first what the rest of the North could postpone: preach the same gospel in two languages to one people. Preachers were appointed for Danish parishes and German parishes alike, the catechism was printed in both tongues, and the cathedral town of Slesvig kept a German-speaking chapter under an evangelical superintendent. The dictionary records the duchy because it is a small, early instance of the universal claim of the gospel over every speech, which is not a modern discovery but a Pentecost fact. The crowd at Jerusalem were astonished at precisely this, asking “how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?” (Act 2:8). The answer heaven gives is that the thing preached is too large for one language, and that no tongue has a prior claim upon it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a tongue as the instrument of taste and speech, and by extension a language; a nation as a body of people inhabiting the same country under the same government; and a kindred as relation by birth, consanguinity.
webster_full: TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech in man and other animals; also, a language; the whole sum of words used by a nation.
NATION, n. [L. natio.] A body of people inhabiting the same country, or united under the same sovereign or government.
KINDRED, n. Relation by birth; consanguinity; also, relatives by blood.
MULTITUDE, n. [L. multitudo.] The state of being many; a great number of persons or things collectively.
scriptures: Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
Act 2:11
Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.
Rev 7:9

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
Rev 5:9

And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation;
corruption_summary: The bilingual border duchy, reformed before Denmark itself, which preached one gospel in Danish and German at once.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the binding of the gospel to a nation, so that to receive Christ a man must also receive somebody else's language, liturgy and loyalties. Slesvig could not afford the error and did not commit it. The same catechism was printed twice because the doctrine, not the dialect, was the thing being handed over.

The principle to recover is that Christ has purchased a people out of every tongue and will be praised in all of them. The Pentecost crowd heard the wonderful works of God in their own languages, saying that “we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11). John sees the end of it, “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9), standing before the Lamb. And the new song names the price and the extent together, that He has “redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation” (Rev 5:9).

Greek dialektos (G1258) — a dialect, the speech of a region; Acts 2:8.
Greek phule (G5443) — a tribe, a clan, a kindred; Revelation 5:9.
Greek ethnos (G1484) — a nation, a people; Revelation 7:9.
Greek agorazo (G59) — to buy in the market, to purchase, to redeem; Revelation 5:9.

“a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9) — the catechism printed in both languages.
“redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation” (Rev 5:9) — reformed before Denmark proper.

pos: n. (city of Scania; archiepiscopal see of all Scandinavia from 1104, and from 1537 an evangelical bishopric)
etymology: From Old Norse lundr, a grove; the name of the sacred wood that stood before the cathedral.
biblical_def: Lund was the ecclesiastical capital of the North. Made an archbishopric in 1104, it held the primacy over Denmark, Sweden, Norway and the Atlantic colonies, and its archbishop was for four centuries the greatest churchman between Hamburg and the Arctic. The Reformation dismantled that primacy. The last Roman archbishop fled, and in 1537 Frands Vormordsen was installed not as metropolitan but as superintendent of Scania, an overseer of parishes under the word. When Scania passed to Sweden in 1658 the city received a university, and Lund became a seat of Lutheran learning rather than of jurisdiction. The dictionary records Lund because the surrender of a primacy is one of the Reformation's plainest doctrinal acts. The church has a Head, and He is not resident in any see. Paul says that the Father “gave him to be the head over all things to the church” (Eph 1:22), and a church that has grasped this cannot afterwards install a visible substitute without contradicting its own confession.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a primate as the chief ecclesiastic in a national church; preeminence as superiority in excellence or in place; and a head as the chief or principal person, a leader or chief magistrate.
webster_full: PRIMATE, n. [L. primas.] The chief ecclesiastic in the church; an archbishop who has jurisdiction over other bishops.
PREEMINENCE, n. Superiority in excellence; distinction in something commendable; precedence; priority of place.
HEAD, n. The chief or principal person of a company or multitude; a chief, a leader, a principal.
GROVE, n. A wood of small extent; a cluster of trees; in Scripture, often a place of idolatrous worship.
scriptures: Eph 1:22
And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church,
Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
Mat 23:8
But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.
And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.
corruption_summary: The archiepiscopal see of all Scandinavia from 1104; its primacy surrendered in 1537 for a superintendency under the word.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the papal claim itself, of which Lund was the northern miniature: a visible head with jurisdiction over other bishops, holding a primacy by office rather than by gift. The Reformation did not abolish oversight, but it denied that oversight can be a monarchy, and it put the title of head beyond any man's reach. Where that denial weakens, the structure returns under new names, and a conference or a presidency acquires what a cathedral once held.

The principle to recover is the sole headship of Christ over His church. Paul makes it exclusive and total: “And he is the head of the body, the church” (Col 1:18), the firstborn from the dead, that in all things He might have the preeminence. Christ forbade the honorific that establishes such rank among brethren, saying “be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ” (Mat 23:8). And Peter, writing to elders, keeps his own office beneath another, for the reward comes “when the chief Shepherd shall appear” (1Pe 5:4).

roots_lines: Greek kephale (G2776) — a head, and figuratively one in authority; Ephesians 1:22.

Greek kathegetes (G2519) — a guide, a master, a teacher; Matthew 23:10.
Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly, the church called out; Colossians 1:18.

“And he is the head of the body, the church” (Col 1:18) — Vormordsen installed as superintendent, not metropolitan.
“be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ” (Mat 23:8) — a university seat after 1658.

pos: n. (Danish theologian, 1513–1600; professor at Copenhagen, called the teacher of Denmark, deprived of his chair in 1579)
etymology: From Danish Hemmingsen, son of Hemming; Latinised Nicolaus Hemmingius.
biblical_def: Niels Hemmingsen was the ablest theologian Denmark produced in the sixteenth century and the only one with a European reputation. A pupil of Melanchthon at Wittenberg, he taught at Copenhagen for thirty-five years, wrote on logic, law, preaching and the Epistles, and was read in England and Scotland as well as in the North; students came to him from Norway, Iceland and Scotland. His trouble came over the Lord's Supper. Following Melanchthon rather than the stricter Lutherans, he held that Christ is received spiritually by faith and not by the mouth of the body, which is the Reformed position; pressure from the Saxon court obliged Frederick II to deprive him of his chair in 1579, and he lived his last twenty-one years as a canon at Roskilde. The dictionary records him because his case marks the exact boundary the Reformed and the Lutherans could not cross together. Paul's question settles the doctrine on the side Hemmingsen took: “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?” (1Co 10:16). Communion is the word, and communion is by faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines communion as fellowship, mutual intercourse, and the celebration of the Lord's supper; to quicken as to make alive, to revive; and a sacrament as an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace.
webster_full: COMMUNION, n. [L. communio.] Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; also, the celebration of the Lord's supper.
QUICKEN, v.t. To make alive; to vivify; to revive or resuscitate, as from death.
SACRAMENT, n. [L. sacramentum.] An outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace; among Protestants, baptism and the Lord's supper.
FAITH, n. [L. fides.] Belief; the assent of the mind to the truth of what is declared by another, resting on his authority and veracity.
scriptures: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
Joh 6:63
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
Joh 6:35
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
corruption_summary: Melanchthon's best northern pupil, deprived of his Copenhagen chair in 1579 for holding the Reformed doctrine of the Supper.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions stand on either side of Hemmingsen, and the dictionary rejects both. Rome teaches that the elements are changed into the body and blood, so that the sacrifice is repeated; Lutheran sacramental union attaches the body to the bread so that the unbeliever receives Christ with his teeth. Against both, the Reformed confession holds that the signs remain bread and wine and that Christ is truly present to faith. The third error, bare memorialism, empties the ordinance of presence altogether and is equally wrong.

The principle to recover is that the benefit is received by faith and the instrument of receiving is the soul, not the mouth. Christ Himself laid down the rule in the discourse that most tempts a carnal reading: “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63). He defines the eating as coming and believing, saying “I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger” (Joh 6:35). And Paul keeps the rite commemorative and forward-looking at once, for as often as we eat and drink “ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26).

Greek kataggello (G2605) — to proclaim, to shew forth, to declare openly; 1 Corinthians 11:26.

“It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63) — deprived under Saxon pressure, 1579.
“I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger” (Joh 6:35) — twenty-one last years a canon at Roskilde.

pos: n. (Danish theologian, 1585–1652; bishop of Zealand and author of the great Danish Lutheran system of divinity)
etymology: From Danish Brochmand, a family name; the given name Jesper a northern form of Caspar.
biblical_def: Jesper Brochmand was the systematiser of Danish Lutheran orthodoxy. Professor at Copenhagen, then bishop of Zealand from 1639 until his death, he wrote the Universae theologiae systema, the one Danish work of dogmatics of the century that scholars outside Denmark used, and also the book by which he actually reached his countrymen: an enormous volume of household sermons on the Gospels and Epistles, which stood in Danish and Norwegian farmhouses for two hundred years and was read aloud on Sundays where no minister could be reached. The dictionary records him because he held together the two things that most often come apart, a complete system and a plain sermon, and did not think the second beneath the first. Paul claimed exactly this completeness at Ephesus: “For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27). A system of divinity is nothing more than that declaration put in order so it can be taught, and a household sermon is the same counsel brought within reach of a farmer who will never see a university.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines doctrine as whatever is taught, a principle or position in any science; a system as a regular union of principles arranged in due order; and counsel as advice, deliberation, and the purpose or design of God.
webster_full: DOCTRINE, n. [L. doctrina.] Whatever is taught; principles or positions in any branch of knowledge; whatever is laid down as true by an instructor.
SYSTEM, n. [Gr. to set together.] An assemblage of things adjusted into a regular whole; a regular union of principles or parts arranged in due order.
COUNSEL, n. [L. consilium.] Advice; opinion or instruction given upon request; also, purpose, design, the plan of God's providence.
SOUND, adj. Right; correct; well founded; free from error; orthodox.
scriptures: For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Tit 2:1
But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine:
Rom 6:17
But God be thanked, that ye were the servants of sin, but ye have obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine which was delivered you.
corruption_summary: Bishop of Zealand and author of the Danish system of divinity, and of the household sermons read in farmhouses for two centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the modern divorce between systematic theology and the ordinary congregation, which leaves the first unread and the second unfed. Where doctrine is treated as a specialism, preaching degenerates into comment on experience, and the hearer who wants to know what the church believes has nowhere to go. Brochmand wrote for both audiences out of one set of convictions, and the farmhouse volume outlasted the Latin one.

The principle to recover is that sound doctrine has a shape which can be handed on whole. Paul gives Timothy a pattern to keep, not merely a set of opinions: “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me” (2Ti 1:13). He makes it the minister's plain business, “But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine” (Tit 2:1). And he can thank God for a congregation's obedience to a doctrinal mould, that “ye have obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine which was delivered you” (Rom 6:17).

pos: n. (Danish nobleman and lay theologian, 1574–1642; called the Learned, founder of the school at Rosenholm)
biblical_def: Holger Rosenkrantz was a Danish magnate who turned his manor into a school. A privy councillor who withdrew from office to study divinity, he gathered young noblemen at Rosenholm, taught them himself, corresponded with theologians across Protestant Europe, and wrote a good deal on faith, repentance and the Christian life. His learning was real and his piety was not in question, but his doctrine of faith was. Pressing against a dead orthodoxy in which assent was mistaken for trust, he so defined faith as to include the new obedience within it, and the Copenhagen faculty judged that he had confused justification with sanctification; he was obliged to withdraw his books, and he died out of favour in 1642. The dictionary records him as an honest man wrong on a central point. The error is instructive because its motive was good. Paul will not let the two stand together in the ground of salvation: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8). Works follow; they never contribute.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines faith as the assent of the mind to the truth of what is declared by another, and in theology the assent of the mind to the truth of divine revelation; grace as the free unmerited love and favour of God; and works as actions performed.
webster_full: FAITH, n. [L. fides.] Belief; the assent of the mind to the truth of what is declared by another, resting on his authority and veracity; in theology, the assent of the mind to the truth of divine revelation.
GRACE, n. [L. gratia.] The free unmerited love and favor of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
WORK, n. Labor; employment; that which is produced by labor or by mental exertion; action; deed.
WORKMANSHIP, n. The skill of a workman; also, that which is effected, made or produced; the work done.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Eph 2:10
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
Jam 2:18
Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.
corruption_summary: The learned Danish nobleman whose school at Rosenholm outlived his doctrine of faith, which drew obedience into justification.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the one Rosenkrantz fell into from the right side of the road: a reaction against formal orthodoxy that repairs dead assent by adding obedience to the definition of faith. It still happens, and it still produces the same result, a believer who cannot tell whether he is accepted because of Christ or because of the change Christ has worked in him. The Roman doctrine of infused righteousness reaches the same end by design; the pious reaction reaches it by accident.

The principle to recover is the order: grace, then faith, then works, each in its own place and none doing another's office. Paul excludes the boast absolutely, saying salvation is “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9). He then puts works where they belong, as the thing we are made for and not the thing we are saved by, for “we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works” (Eph 2:10). James is not in conflict with this but is answering a different claim, demanding of the empty professor, “shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works” (Jam 2:18).

pos: n. (the Copenhagen Confession of 1530; forty-three articles presented by the Danish evangelical preachers to the national assembly)
etymology: Latin confessio, a confession, and Hafnia, the Latin name of Copenhagen.
biblical_def: The Confessio Hafnica is the first confession of faith the Danish Reformation produced. In July 1530 the national assembly at Copenhagen summoned the evangelical preachers to answer for themselves, and twenty-one of them, Hans Tausen chief among them, submitted forty-three articles stating what they taught: the authority of Scripture, justification by faith, the two sacraments, the rejection of the mass as a sacrifice, of monastic vows, of the invocation of saints, and of clerical celibacy. The bishops answered with twenty-seven articles of their own and demanded a disputation in Latin; the preachers insisted that the matter be argued in Danish before the people whose souls were in question, and the assembly broke up without a verdict. The dictionary records the document because confession is not an optional sequel to belief but part of it. Christ ties His own acknowledgment of a man to the man's acknowledgment of Him: “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:32). Forty-three articles in Danish were that verse obeyed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession as the acknowledgment of a crime or fault, and also a formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; an article as a distinct part or particular; and to profess as to declare openly.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. [L. confessio.] The acknowledgment of a crime, fault or something to one's disadvantage; also, a formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised.
ARTICLE, n. [L. articulus.] A single clause in a contract, account, system of regulations, treaty or other writing; a particular; a distinct part.
PROFESS, v.t. [L. profiteor.] To make open declaration of; to avow or acknowledge; to declare in strong terms.
DISPUTATION, n. [L. disputatio.] The act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition to something.
scriptures: Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.
For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
Act 4:20
For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.
corruption_summary: Forty-three articles laid before the Danish assembly in 1530 by twenty-one evangelical preachers, who demanded the debate be held in Danish.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the preference for an unwritten faith, defended as humility and practised as evasion. A church that will not state its articles cannot be held to them, cannot be reformed by them, and cannot hand them on; and the demand for a confession is treated as narrowness precisely by those whose position would not survive being written down. The Danish bishops wanted the argument in Latin for the same reason, to keep it among experts.

The principle to recover is that saving faith is confessing faith, and that it confesses publicly and in the common tongue. Paul joins the inward and the outward in one sentence: “For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom 10:10). He reminds Timothy of a confession made in the open, that he “hast professed a good profession before many witnesses” (1Ti 6:12). And Peter and John, forbidden to speak, answer with the plainest reason there is: “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20).

pos: n. (Danish bishop and author, 1698–1764; bishop of Bergen, and author of the catechism explanation used in Denmark and Norway for two centuries)
etymology: Latinised Danish Pontoppidan, from Broby, bridge town; pons, bridge, and oppidum, town.
biblical_def: Erik Pontoppidan was a pietist bishop who gave the North its most widely used book of instruction. Court chaplain, professor, and from 1748 bishop of Bergen in Norway, he wrote on antiquities, folklore and natural history, but his lasting work was Sandhed til Gudfrygtighed, Truth unto Godliness, published in 1737: an explanation of Luther's Small Catechism in seven hundred and fifty-nine questions, which became the standard text for confirmation in Denmark and Norway and was still being learned by heart in Norwegian and Norwegian-American parishes in the twentieth century. Emigrants carried it to the American Midwest. The dictionary records him because his title states the right relation between doctrine and life, and states it in the apostle's own order. Paul describes his commission as being for the faith of the elect and “the acknowledging of the truth which is after godliness” (Tit 1:1). Truth comes first and godliness follows from it; a catechism is simply that order made teachable to a child.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines godliness as piety, belief in God with reverence and obedience; a catechism as a form of instruction by question and answer; and truth as conformity to fact or reality, exact accordance with that which is.
webster_full: GODLINESS, n. Piety; belief in God, and reverence for his character and laws; a religious life.
CATECHISM, n. [Gr. to instruct by asking questions.] A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
TRUTH, n. Conformity to fact or reality; exact accordance with that which is, or has been, or shall be.
CONFIRMATION, n. The act of confirming or establishing; also, an ecclesiastical rite by which persons are admitted to the full privileges of the church.
scriptures: Tit 1:1
Paul, a servant of God, and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God's elect, and the acknowledging of the truth which is after godliness;
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
According as his divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness, through the knowledge of him that hath called us to glory and virtue:
If any man teach otherwise, and consent not to wholesome words, even the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness;
corruption_summary: Bishop of Bergen; his 1737 Truth unto Godliness was learned by heart in Denmark, Norway and the American Midwest for two centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the inversion of Pontoppidan's title, so that godliness is sought without truth and devotion is cultivated as a mood with no doctrinal content to feed it. Pietism itself ran this risk and sometimes incurred it, setting the warm heart against the exact confession; where that happens the next generation has the warmth without the reason for it, and loses both. Pontoppidan's own remedy was seven hundred and fifty-nine questions with answers.

The principle to recover is that godliness is the fruit of doctrine and is profitable beyond anything else a man can train. Paul weighs it against the body's discipline: “For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things” (1Ti 4:8). Peter grounds the whole life in what has been given and known, since divine power “hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness” (2Pe 1:3). And Paul marks the false teacher by his refusal of the doctrine that produces it, the man who consents not to wholesome words “and to the doctrine which is according to godliness” (1Ti 6:3).
